title: Multi-Leader & Leaderless Replication
description: Explore replication beyond single-leader setups — multi-leader conflict resolution, CRDTs, and Dynamo-style quorum reads and writes.

segments.text: Single-leader replication is simple and well understood. But what if your leader is in Virginia and your users are in Tokyo? Every write crosses an ocean. Today we explore architectures that eliminate the single-leader bottleneck entirely.

In multi-leader replication, multiple nodes accept writes independently. Each datacenter has its own leader. Users in Tokyo write to the Tokyo leader, users in London write to the London leader. Each leader replicates to the others asynchronously.

But what happens when two users update the same record at the same time in different datacenters? User A changes a name in Tokyo while user B changes it in London. When the leaders sync, they have two conflicting versions. Which one wins?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you decide which conflicting write should win?

segments.text: There are several strategies. Last-writer-wins uses timestamps to pick the latest write, but clocks can be wrong. Custom merge functions let application logic resolve conflicts. Or you can keep both versions and let the user decide.

The most elegant approach is CRDTs — Conflict-free Replicated Data Types. These are data structures mathematically designed so that concurrent updates always merge automatically without conflicts. Counters, sets, and maps can all be CRDTs.

A CRDT counter works by having each node track its own increment count. The total is the sum of all nodes. Two nodes can increment simultaneously without conflict because addition is commutative. The merge always converges to the correct total.

Now let's go even further. Leaderless replication has no leaders at all. Every node is equal. The client sends writes to multiple nodes simultaneously, and reads from multiple nodes to get the latest value. This is the Dynamo-style approach.

The magic formula is R plus W greater than N. If you have N replicas, write to W of them and read from R of them. As long as R plus W exceeds N, at least one node in your read set has the latest write. That overlap guarantees consistency.
segments.thought_prompt: With 3 replicas, what values of R and W satisfy R+W>N? What are the trade-offs of each choice?

segments.text: With N equals 3, you could set W equals 2 and R equals 2. That tolerates one node failure for both reads and writes. Or set W equals 3 and R equals 1 for fast reads but slower writes. The quorum is tunable to your access pattern.

Cassandra and Riak use leaderless replication with tunable quorums. Google's collaborative editing tools use CRDTs. Multi-leader replication powers CouchDB and MySQL Group Replication. Each approach fits different requirements.

Single-leader is simplest but has a bottleneck. Multi-leader gives geographic distribution but adds conflict complexity. Leaderless gives maximum availability with tunable consistency. Choose based on your latency, consistency, and availability requirements.
